requirements.requirement: /srv/drop exists as a directory with sticky bit set, world-writable, owned by root:root
requirements.summary: stat confirms drwxrwxrwt root:root both immediately after creation and again after cleanup, matching expected mode 1777.

requirements.requirement: Directory is shared and writable by all users (any user can create files)
requirements.summary: Two distinct real users (dropuserA, dropuserB) each successfully created files in /srv/drop.

requirements.requirement: Users cannot remove files owned by other users, but can remove their own
requirements.summary: dropuserB's attempt to delete dropuserA's file failed with 'Operation not permitted' (sticky bit behavior), while dropuserA successfully deleted its own file. This was demonstrated twice (pre- and post-restart) with consistent results.

requirements.requirement: Configuration and behavior persist across a node restart (implicit durability expectation for a filesystem configuration change)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id (d22a0434...) and post-restart boot_id (fef8c35e...) differ, confirming an actual reboot occurred. Post-restart, /srv/drop retained mode 1777 root:root and the full cross-user create/delete-blocked/self-delete-allowed test passed identically to the pre-restart run.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task were directly demonstrated: /srv/drop was created with sticky-bit mode 1777 owned by root:root, verified functionally with two real users showing shared writability and sticky-bit protection against cross-user deletion, and this behavior along with the directory's permissions survived a full node restart confirmed by a changed boot_id. Test accounts were removed and confirmed absent. The only shortcoming is a few small leftover temp/log files in /tmp from testing and the reboot command that were not cleaned up, a minor hygiene issue rather than a functional one.
limitations: Package-health observation shows an unmodified pre-existing 'U var/lib/chrony/chrony.drift' entry in both before-prepare and after-executor snapshots; this predates the executor's work and is not attributable to it.
Listening-sockets diff reflects the expected DHCP lease/IP and PID change from the reboot, not an executor-introduced network exposure change.

operational_hygiene.summary: Test users (dropuserA/dropuserB) and their home directories were created twice (pre- and post-restart) for functional verification and were fully removed both times, confirmed by a leftover-account grep returning none. However, three small stderr/log files (/tmp/err, /tmp/reboot.log, /tmp/rmA.err) created during testing and the reboot sequence were never cleaned up, per the after-executor temporary-files diff showing them added with no corresponding removal. This is bounded, low-risk residue (small text files in /tmp) rather than a broad or destructive mutation, but is nonetheless unnecessary leftover state from the executor's own diagnostic/reboot commands (cmd-11d40c4a2e824788, cmd-17e375dad8d04579, cmd-64fecc08cc624b5a). No failed services, package-state damage, or unsafe exposure was introduced; the listening-sockets diff reflects only the expected DHCP address/PID change from the reboot, not an executor-caused exposure change.
